title: Nothing goes here: subject–verb, verb–object, paired coordinates, essential clauses
subtitle: Boundaries · 32 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **32 of the official questions in Boundaries are this one** — 15 Easy, 8 Medium, 9 Hard.
Most versions sit at the Easy tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- One choice has no punctuation at all, and the others add a comma, colon, dash, or semicolon at a spot that feels like a breath pause.
- Examples are right before the main verb after a long subject, right after a verb, before 'and' joining two parallel noun or 'how/what' elements, or before a restrictive 'that' clause.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Name the grammatical relationship across the blank: is it a subject and its verb, a verb and its object, two parallel parts joined by 'and', or a noun and its identifying 'that' clause?
- 2) If it is any of these, choose the option with no punctuation.
- 3) Check that the no-punctuation version reads as one sentence with a single main clause.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: A long subject or a long object makes you want to 'breathe' with a comma.
Commas never separate a subject from its verb, a verb from its object, two coordinated non-clauses, or a noun from an essential 'that' clause.

sections.heading: You are losing these
